{{Short description|Number that is the sum of the factorials of its digits}}
In [[number theory]], a '''factorion''' in a given [[number base]] <math>b</math> is a [[natural number]] that equals the sum of the [[factorial]]s of its [[numerical digit|digits]].<ref name="A014080">{{Citation|last=Sloane|first=Neil|website=[[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences]]|title=A014080|url=https://oeis.org/A014080}}</ref><ref name="Gardner">{{Citation|last=Gardner|first=Martin|chapter=Factorial Oddities|date=1978|publisher=Vintage Books|pages=61 and 64|title=Mathematical Magic Show: More Puzzles, Games, Diversions, Illusions and Other Mathematical Sleight-Of-Mind|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RcnbvQEACAAJ&q=Mathematical+Magic+Show:+More+Puzzles,+Games,+Diversions,+Illusions+and+Other+Mathematical+Sleight-Of-Mind|isbn=9780394726236}}</ref><ref name="Madachy">{{Citation|last=Madachy|first=Joseph S.|year=1979|publisher=Dover Publications|page=167|title=Madachy's Mathematical Recreations|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UvpUAAAAYAAJ&q=Madachy%27s+Mathematical+Recreations|isbn=9780486237626}}</ref> The name factorion was coined by the author [[Clifford A. Pickover]].<ref name="Pickover">{{Citation|last=Pickover|first=Clifford A.|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|year=1995|pages=169–171 and 319–320|title=Keys to Infinity|chapter=The Loneliness of the Factorions|via=Google Books|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oXIFAAAACAAJ&q=Keys+to+Infinity|isbn=9780471193340}}</ref>

==Definition==
Let <math>n</math> be a natural number.  For a base <math>b > 1</math>, we define the '''sum of the factorials of the digits'''<ref name="Gupta">{{Citation|last=Gupta|first=Shyam S.|title=Sum of the Factorials of the Digits of Integers|journal=The Mathematical Gazette|publisher=The Mathematical Association|volume=88|issue=512|year=2004|pages=258–261 |jstor=3620841|doi=10.1017/S0025557200174996|s2cid=125854033|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="A061602">{{Citation|last=Sloane|first=Neil|website=[[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences]]|title=A061602|url=https://oeis.org/A061602}}</ref> of <math>n</math>, <math>\operatorname{SFD}_b : \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}</math>, to be the following:
:<math>\operatorname{SFD}_b(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{k - 1} d_i!.</math>
where <math>k = \lfloor \log_b n \rfloor + 1</math> is the number of digits in the number in base <math>b</math>, <math>n!</math> is the [[factorial]] of <math>n</math> and 
:<math>d_i = \frac{n \bmod{b^{i+1}} - n \bmod{b^{i}}}{b^{i}}</math> 
is the value of the <math>i</math>th digit of the number. A natural number <math>n</math> is a <math>b</math>-'''factorion''' if it is a [[Fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]] for <math>\operatorname{SFD}_b</math>, i.e. if <math>\operatorname{SFD}_b(n) = n</math>.<ref name="Abbott">{{Citation|first=Steve|last=Abbott|title=SFD Chains and Factorion Cycles|journal=The Mathematical Gazette|publisher=The Mathematical Association|volume=88|issue=512|year=2004|pages=261–263 |jstor=3620842|doi=10.1017/S002555720017500X|s2cid=99976100}}</ref> <math>1</math> and <math>2</math> are fixed points for all bases <math>b</math>, and thus are '''trivial factorions''' for all <math>b</math>, and all other factorions are '''nontrivial factorions'''. 

For example, the number 145 in base <math>b = 10</math> is a factorion because <math>145 = 1! + 4! + 5!</math>. 

For <math>b = 2</math>, the sum of the factorials of the digits is simply the number of digits <math>k</math> in the base 2 representation since <math>0! = 1! = 1</math>. 

A natural number <math>n</math> is a '''sociable factorion''' if it is a [[periodic point]] for <math>\operatorname{SFD}_b</math>, where <math>\operatorname{SFD}_b^c(n) = n</math> for a positive [[integer]] <math>c</math>, and forms a [[Periodic sequence|cycle]] of period <math>c</math>. A factorion is a sociable factorion with <math>c = 1</math>, and a '''amicable factorion''' is a sociable factorion with <math>c = 2</math>.<ref name="A214285">{{Citation|last=Sloane|first=Neil|website=[[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences]]|title=A214285|url=https://oeis.org/A214285}}</ref><ref name="A254499">{{Citation|last=Sloane|first=Neil|website=[[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences]]|title=A254499|url=https://oeis.org/A254499}}</ref>

All natural numbers <math>n</math> are [[periodic point#iterated function|preperiodic points]] for <math>\operatorname{SFD}_b</math>, regardless of the base. This is because all natural numbers of base <math>b</math> with <math>k</math> digits satisfy <math>b^{k-1} \leq n < b^{k}</math>. Given that each of the <math>k</math> digits is at most <math>b-1</math>, <math>\operatorname{SFD}_b \leq (b-1)!k</math>. However, when <math>k \geq b</math>, then <math>b^{k-1} > (b-1)!(k)</math> for <math>b > 2</math>, so any <math>n</math> will satisfy <math>n > \operatorname{SFD}_b(n)</math> until <math>n < b^b</math>. There are finitely many natural numbers less than <math>b^b</math>, so the number is guaranteed to reach a periodic point or a fixed point less than <math> b^b</math>, making it a preperiodic point. For <math>b = 2</math>, the number of digits <math>k \leq n</math> for any number, once again, making it a preperiodic point. This means also that there are a finite number of factorions and [[Periodic sequence|cycles]] for any given base <math>b</math>. 

The number of iterations <math>i</math> needed for <math>\operatorname{SFD}_b^i(n)</math> to reach a fixed point is the <math>\operatorname{SFD}_b</math> function's [[persistence of a number|persistence]] of <math>n</math>, and undefined if it never reaches a fixed point.

==Factorions for {{Math|{{math|SFD<sub>''b''</sub>}}}}==
===''b'' = (''m'' − 1)!===
Let <math>m</math> be a positive integer and the number base <math>b = (m - 1)!</math>. Then:
*<math>n_1 = mb + 1</math> is a factorion for <math>\operatorname{SFD}_b</math> for all <math>m\geq 4</math>.
{{Math proof|title=Proof|drop=hidden|proof=
Let the digits of <math>n_1 = d_1 b + d_0</math> be <math>d_1 = m</math>, and <math>d_0 = 1.</math> Then
: <math>\operatorname{SFD}_b(n_1) = d_1! + d_0!</math>
:: <math> = m! + 1!</math>
:: <math> = m(m - 1)! + 1</math>
:: <math> = d_1 b + d_0</math>
:: <math> = n_1</math>
Thus <math>n_1</math> is a factorion for <math>F_b</math> for all <math>k</math>. 
}}
*<math>n_2 = mb + 2</math> is a factorion for <math>\operatorname{SFD}_b</math> for all <math>m\geq 4</math>. 
{{Math proof|title=Proof|drop=hidden|proof=
Let the digits of <math>n_2 = d_1 b + d_0</math> be <math>d_1 = m</math>, and <math>d_0 = 2</math>. Then
: <math>\operatorname{SFD}_b(n_2) = d_1! + d_0!</math>
:: <math> = m! + 2!</math>
:: <math> = m(m - 1)! + 2</math>
:: <math> = d_1 b + d_0</math>
:: <math> = n_2</math>
Thus <math>n_2</math> is a factorion for <math>F_b</math> for all <math>k</math>. 
}}

===''b'' = ''m''! − ''m'' + 1===
Let <math>k</math> be a positive integer and the number base <math>b = m! - m + 1</math>. Then:
*<math>n_1 = b + m</math> is a factorion for <math>\operatorname{SFD}_b</math> for all <math>m\geq 3</math>.
{{Math proof|title=Proof|drop=hidden|proof=
Let the digits of <math>n_1 = d_1 b + d_0</math> be <math>d_1 = 1</math>, and <math>d_0 = m</math>. Then
: <math>\operatorname{SFD}_b(n_1) = d_1! + d_0!</math>
:: <math> = 1! + m!</math>
:: <math> = m! + 1 - m + m</math>
:: <math> = 1(m! - m + 1) + m</math>
:: <math> = d_1 b + d_0</math>
:: <math> = n_1</math>
Thus <math>n_1</math> is a factorion for <math>F_b</math> for all <math>m</math>. 
}}
